Revised PR addressing Responsible‑AI review (standard-revenue case). Summary of changes & artifacts included:

1) Data minimization / schema (no direct PII)
- Updated migration: migrations/2026_add_revenue_table.sql — revenue_snapshots schema contains: id (uuid), tenant_id (uuid), snapshot_time (timestamp), cohort_keys (jsonb), account_hash (text), revenue_cents (bigint), aggregated_count (int), metadata (jsonb).
- Removed any direct identifiers (no emails, names). account_hash is a HMAC-SHA256 of account_id using a per-environment HMAC key from KMS. Schema file and sample sanitized records: docs/artifacts/revenue_snapshot_schema.md and docs/artifacts/sample_records_sanitized.json
- Sample sanitized record:
  {"id":"...","tenant_id":"111e2222-3333-4444-5555-666677778888","snapshot_time":"2026-07-01T00:00:00Z","cohort_keys":{"country":"US","plan":"pro"},"account_hash":"hmac:sha256:ab12...","revenue_cents":12345,"aggregated_count":42}

2) Re-identification risk & aggregation safeguards (DPIA)
- Added DPIA and short re-identification assessment: docs/artifacts/reidentification_dpia.md
- Enforced aggregation safeguards in RevenueCalculator and SQL: minimum_group_size = 10 (configurable via ENV REVENUE_MIN_GROUP_SIZE). Queries that would return aggregated_count < 10 are suppressed (return 'suppressed' flag) and revenue values are rounded to nearest $10 (1000 cents) for small cohorts. Rationale: protects against singling out while preserving analytic utility for business reporting.
- Implemented suppression/rounding in src/services/RevenueCalculator.py and tests in tests/unit/revenue_aggregation_tests.py

3) Access controls & auth evidence
- Auth middleware: src/middleware/auth.py (JWT bearer validation, tenant scoping) and src/controllers/RevenueController.py uses @require_tenant and @require_role('report_reader') decorators.
- Authorization tests: tests/integration/authorization/revenue_auth_tests.py — covers permitted tenant access, denied cross-tenant access, RBAC denial for non-report roles, and examples of denied requests (401/403 responses recorded).
- Example denied request logged in tests: docs/artifacts/denied_examples.md

4) Logging & redaction
- Confirmed logs do not contain PII. Logging format in docs/artifacts/logging_format.md: JSON lines containing request_id, timestamp, tenant_id (uuid only), endpoint, user_id_hash (HMAC), action, outcome. account_hash and other sensitive fields are redacted in access logs.
- Audit logging design: src/services/audit_logger.py writes immutable audit entries to audit_log table with columns (id, tenant_id, actor_hash, action, resource, timestamp). Retention and access controls described below.

5) Retention & deletion
- Retention policy: revenue_snapshots retained 90 days by default; archived to long-term encrypted storage after 90 days; snapshots older than 365 days purged unless legal hold. Audit logs retained 1 year (configurable). Procedures for DSAR/deletion documented in docs/artifacts/retention_and_dsar.md and operations playbook: docs/ops/delete_snapshot_playbook.md

6) Consent / lawful basis
- Statement of alignment: docs/artifacts/consent_and_legal.md — confirms revenue analytics covered under our product ToS/consents for aggregated reporting; legal team sign-off included in the doc. If additional constraints apply per tenant, endpoints respect tenant opt-outs and are filtered accordingly.

7) Storage protections
- Encryption in transit: TLS 1.2+ enforced at API and DB connections. In-rest: DB encrypted at rest (provider-managed AES-256). account_hash is HMAC (one-way); if identifiers were stored, column-level encryption using KMS is implemented for sensitive columns — see migrations and src/db/column_encryption.py. Key management: AWS KMS (or equivalent) with rotation policies documented in docs/artifacts/key_management.md

8) Adversarial / auxiliary risks
- Controls to prevent linking: rate limits per-tenant (10 requests/min default, configurable) implemented in src/middleware/rate_limit.py; query restrictions: disallow arbitrary combination of filters that would isolate individuals (block queries that specify cohort of size < minimum_group_size at filter time). Query builder only allows predefined cohort dimensions (docs/allowed_filters.md). Endpoints return suppression/rounded values for small cohorts.

9) Artifacts & code locations (raw-SQL sections highlighted)
- Controller & data-access: src/controllers/RevenueController.py, src/services/RevenueCalculator.py, src/db/revenue_dao.py (raw SQL in queries flagged with /* RAW SQL */ comments).
- Migrations: migrations/2026_add_revenue_table.sql (updated)

- Authorization tests: tests/integration/authorization/revenue_auth_tests.py
- New dependencies: python-cryptography (for HMAC utilities), aws-kms-client (KMS wrapper), ratelimit-lib. Listed in requirements.txt and docs/artifacts/new_dependencies.md
- Re-identification/DPIA: docs/artifacts/reidentification_dpia.md

10) Operational recommendations
- Rate limits (10 req/min per tenant default), caching of generated snapshots via Redis with TTL, snapshot generation is auditable and restricted to 'snapshot_generator' role. Implemented caching in src/services/snapshot_cache.py and snapshot generation gating in src/services/snapshot_scheduler.py.

Tests & CI
- Added unit and integration tests: tests/unit/* and tests/integration/* (authorization, aggregation, suppression behavior). CI runs include DPIA checklist validation and dependency scanning.

A) Required mitigations / policy changes (privacy-focused)
1. Keying & HMAC hardening
   - Provide KMS key policy, rotation schedule, ACLs (who can Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign), and estimated KMS latency/SLA. Use per-environment keys and restrict key use to a minimal service account.
   - Treat account_hash as pseudonymized data but assume attacker with known-plaintext (account_id) can brute-force if account_id entropy is low. Mitigate by: (a) HMAC using a KMS-managed symmetric key plus a per-environment secret (pepper) stored in KMS, or (b) using an intentionally slow KDF (e.g., HKDF+PBKDF2/Argon2) before storing, or (c) tokenization/envelope encryption with KMS. Document which approach is used and why.
   - Provide a rekey/revocation/re-hashing plan: how to rotate keys, rederive account_hashes, and handle in-flight queries; include rollback and containment steps for key compromise.

2. Small-cohort suppression & anti-enumeration
   - Strengthen protections beyond a static REVENUE_MIN_GROUP_SIZE=10: enforce suppression when any combination of filters would yield counts < MIN, and deny responses that could be intersected to isolate individuals.
   - Implement and test query-budgeting and query-graph analysis to detect chained/narrowing queries and rate-limit/block suspicious query patterns (per-actor and per-tenant budgets), with automatic throttling and operator alerts.

3. Migration & privacy hygiene (High)

  9) Cache configuration: Redis/envelope encryption evidence, cache key design rationale, TTLs, and access controls.
 10) Audit_log controls: who can read/write, retention policy, tamper-evidence mechanism.

1. Migration privacy runbook (add exact checklist): run under restricted DB role; disable verbose/logging; do a dry-run in staging; verify no raw IDs are emitted; verify backups; post-migration sanity & privacy checks; rollback commands and validation.
2. KMS compromise & rekey playbook: immediate rotation steps; how to rederive/re-hash or re-tokenize account_hashes; steps to invalidate caches & revoke keys; notification template (Legal/Product/Infra); containment SLA (e.g., initial containment within 1 hour, full rekey within 24–72 hours depending on scale).

label: ToMerger
payload:
A) Required mitigations / prioritized (concise)
1. KMS & account_hash hardening (Critical)
   - Documented per-env KMS keys, key policy, automated rotation schedule, least-privilege IAM, and tested rekey/compromise playbook (re-hash/re-tokenize, cache invalidation, notification SLA).
   - Strengthen account_hash: keep HMAC key only in KMS, AND adopt one mitigation if attacker models or low-entropy IDs are a concern: HMAC+pepper (pepper stored in KMS), deterministic tokenization/envelope encryption via KMS, or pre-hash with a slow KDF. Document chosen approach and rationale.
2. Anti-enumeration protections (High)
   - Enforce server-side suppression after all filters (apply REVENUE_MIN_GROUP_SIZE post-filter), allowlist filterable attributes, enforce per-actor & per-tenant query budgets, and add query-graph detection for chained narrowing. Block/alert suspicious sequences and increase thresholds or require DP/noise for exports.
3. Migration & privacy hygiene (High)
   - Migration runbook must include: run under restricted DB role, no-print/no-dump policy, staging dry-run, masked logs, pre/post privacy checks, backup verification, and rollback commands.
4. Retention & secure deletion (Medium)
   - Baseline: revenue_snapshots TTL = 1 year (configurable); audit_log hot = 90 days then encrypted cold archive per legal; documented secure deletion and DSR verification process.
5. Audit logging & controls (Medium)
   - Audit entries must not contain direct PII (only account_hash), redact sensitive filter values, restrict/monitor reader roles, and use tamper-evidence (append-only/signed entries).
6. Cache & backup protections (Medium)
   - Ensure caches/backups don’t store raw PII, use hashed cache keys, enable envelope encryption for Redis, enforce TTLs and ACLs, and scan backups for leakage.
7. Dependency/SCA controls (Low→Medium)
   - SBOM/pinned versions, CI SCA output, and remediations for any medium findings prior to release.
8. DPIA & legal sign-off (Administrative; required)
   - Complete DPIA documenting re-identification risk and obtain legal/privacy sign-off before production release.

B) Proceed to Arch/DevOps validation? (Decision + required artifacts/tests)
- Decision: Conditional YES to proceed to Arch/DevOps validation, provided the team supplies the artifacts/tests below for Responsible‑AI re-review before final sign-off:
  1) KMS artifacts: key policy doc, rotation schedule, IAM roles allowed, KMS SLA/latency and derived-key caching strategy, and rekey playbook.
  2) account_hash implementation: exact source (path) showing HMAC/KMS usage and any pepper/KDF/tokenization applied.
  3) Short re-identification risk assessment / DPIA: attacker models (known-plaintext, brute-force, external linkage), account_id entropy analysis, and mitigation sufficiency.
  4) migrations/2026_add_revenue_table.sql and migration_runbook.md (privacy checklist, runtime/locks estimate, rollback steps, staging plan).
  5) Raw SQL snippets from src/db/revenue_dao.py to verify parameterization and JSON filter handling.
  6) Evidence of allowed_filters enforcement: query-builder code + unit/integration tests showing disallowed filters rejected.
  7) Enumeration-attack CI tests: simulated chained/narrow filters, asserting suppression/denial and query-budget exhaustion behavior.
  8) CI SCA report and pinned dependency list (SBOM) for new libs (python-cryptography, aws-kms-client, ratelimit-lib, etc.).
  9) Cache config: Redis envelope-encryption evidence, cache key design, TTLs and access controls.
 10) Audit_log controls: who can read/write, retention policy, tamper-evidence mechanism.
- Final Responsible‑AI sign-off withheld until I review these artifacts and the enumeration/suppression tests pass in CI.

C) Concrete playbook/runbook additions required for final sign-off (actionable)
1. Migration privacy runbook: restricted-role execution, dry-run in staging, disable verbose logs, no-stdout of identifiers, pre/post privacy checks, backup verification, rollback commands.
2. KMS compromise & rekey playbook: immediate rotation steps, account_hash re-hash/re-tokenize procedure, cache invalidation steps, revoke keys, stakeholder notification templates (Legal/Product/Infra), containment SLA (e.g., initial containment 1 hour; full recovery 24–72 hours).
3. Enumeration/abuse incident playbook: detection thresholds, automated throttling & block behavior, quarantine flow for suspicious actors, forensic collection steps and retention for supports investigations.
4. DPIA/legal sign-off: include DPIA artifact in release checklist; block release without sign-off.
5. CI/QA: unit tests for suppression & rounding, integration tests simulating chained filters/enumeration, scheduled privacy regression and re-identification scans.
6. Monitoring & alerting: dashboards/alerts for small-cohort frequency, rejected-query counts, unusual query patterns, cache anomalies, and KMS error/latency — include triage playbook.

Re-identification assessment (concise):
- HMAC-SHA256(account_id, KMS_key) provides good protection if the KMS key is secret and account_id has sufficient entropy. If attacker can access KMS or the key is compromised, re-identification is trivial. If account_id space is low-entropy or predictable (e.g., sequential IDs, emails), an offline brute-force/known-plaintext attack could map account_hash values if the key is known or if attacker can call same HMAC oracle. Recommended mitigations: keep key access tightly restricted, prefer envelope tokenization or HMAC+pepper (pepper in KMS), or use a slow KDF/deterministic token service for extra brute-force resistance; require rekey playbook and limit any KMS usage surface to minimal service principal.

Is REVENUE_MIN_GROUP_SIZE=10 + rounding sufficient?
- Not always. Group-size suppression + rounding reduces risk but can be defeated by chained/iterative queries. Additional controls required: server-side post-filter suppression, allowlist of filters, query-budgeting, detection of chained narrowing, higher thresholds for exports, and consider DP/noise for high-risk outputs. Tests simulating enumeration attacks must pass before final sign-off.

Next step request: attach artifacts listed in section B (start with KMS policy, account_hash code, and DPIA) so I can re-review; will issue final Responsible‑AI approval once artifacts/tests and playbook items meet requirements.

2. High — Anti-enumeration & query controls

Security review summary for PR 'Implement standard-revenue calculation':

Overall: Code-quality review passed; security review completed on requested areas and forwarding to Architecture for system-level checks and follow-up on recommendations below.

Findings and recommended actions (priority ordered):
1) Authentication/Authorization (blocking): Ensure GET /api/v1/revenue/standard enforces authentication and RBAC. I found controller hooks present but please confirm: only users with the reporting/finance role may access; verify middleware is applied at route level and cannot be bypassed. Add an automated test for unauthorized access returning 401/403 (see Tests below).

2) Input validation & query-cost limits (high): Validate and bound date-range and pagination server-side. Enforce a maximum date window (e.g., 3 months) and a hard max page_size (e.g., 100) with sensible defaults. Reject requests exceeding limits with 400. Implement server-side query cost protection (max rows scanned). Add tests for overly-large ranges.

3) Rate limiting/abuse (high): This reporting endpoint can be expensive. Apply per-user and per-IP rate limits and/or require higher-tier permissions for heavy queries. Consider async/report generation with cached snapshots for large/long-running requests.

4) SQL/DB safety (mandatory): I inspected service queries—ensure all DB interactions use parameterized ORM methods or prepared statements; reject any raw SQL concatenation. For batch processing/snapshot writes, use bounded batch sizes and explicit transactions with short lock durations.

5) Snapshot storage & PII (high): revenue_snapshots must not contain customer PII (names, emails, payment tokens). If any PII/identifiers are necessary, store only hashed or pseudonymized IDs. Ensure DB encryption-at-rest is enabled for the DB/storage hosting snapshots and enforce least-privilege access to snapshot rows/tables. Consider column-level encryption for sensitive fields.

6) Migration safety (important): Migration should be online-safe: create revenue_snapshots table without locking existing tables, add indexes after table creation, run BACKFILL in small transaction batches, and avoid long-held locks. Provide a rollback path. Test migration under production-like load.

7) Logging & error handling (important): Ensure logs do not include PII, payment info, or raw request bodies. Sanitize and redact sensitive fields in errors and stack traces. Confirm current logging configuration and add tests asserting no PII in logs for test fixtures.

8) Dependencies & supply-chain (medium): I did not spot high-risk new libraries in the diff, but run an SCA (software composition analysis) / dependency-vulnerability scan (e.g., OSS index or Snyk) and pin versions. Monitor for CVEs affecting any new libs used by RevenueCalculator.

9) Tests (action items): Add security-focused tests: unauthenticated request -> 401, authenticated but unauthorized role -> 403, overly-large date ranges -> 400, page_size overflow -> 400, and a load-style integration test ensuring the endpoint honors rate limits/timeouts. Add unit tests asserting snapshots do not include PII fields.

10) Monitoring & alerting: Add metrics for query latency, snapshot generation failures, and abnormal request patterns; alert on spikes which may indicate abuse.

Notes for Architecture team: please validate encryption-at-rest plans, key management (KMS), DB access controls, and whether snapshot storage should be moved to a separate DB/schema with stricter ACLs. Also assess whether async/report generation and a job queue is required to avoid blocking user requests.

Next steps I performed: forwarded review to Architecture for system-level validation and to confirm mitigations above. I will await Merger signals (AgainSecurity or StopSecurity) after Arch's reply.

SecurityReviewer: recommended changes as above; not blocking if auth, input bounds, migration and snapshot-PII mitigations are implemented and tested.

label: ToMerger
payload:
Responsible-AI review for PR 'Implement standard-revenue calculation' — summary, explicit mitigations, CI acceptance tests, and signoff/open concerns.

A) Explicit mitigation recommendations
1) PII minimization & pseudonymization
- Treat the following as PII/indirect identifiers: customer_id, account_number, email, billing_address, phone_number, SSN/NIN, and any free-text fields that may contain identifiers. Treat any external provider IDs mapped to individuals similarly.
- Do NOT store raw PII in revenue_snapshots. Store only pseudonymized IDs using HMAC-SHA256 with a KMS-managed symmetric key (deterministic HMAC for joinability). Use: HMAC-SHA256(key=KMS_key_version, data=<tenant_id||customer_id>), hex/truncate to 128 bits (16 bytes) to limit token size while preserving collision safety. Record the KMS key version id (not the key) in metadata for rotation.
- Key handling: use KMS/CMEK only; keys must be accessible only to a small set of service accounts (no engineers with raw key access). Enforce audit logging on KMS usage. Do not derive HMAC keys from app secrets.

2) Re-identification & aggregation thresholds
- Minimum cohort size (k-anonymity): require k >= 10 for any exported/visible cohort; prefer k >= 20 for public/stable exports. Suppress (do not show) cohort metrics for groups with count < k.
- Time granularity: internal dashboards may use daily buckets only if cohorts are large; for external exports or less-trusted consumers use weekly (7d) minimum bucket size. For small-activity tenants use monthly buckets.
- If precise privacy guarantees are required, adopt differential privacy for aggregates. Start with Laplace mechanism for counts/sums with epsilon <= 1.0 for external/public exports; <= 0.5 for highly sensitive contexts. Document sensitivity used (e.g., max revenue per user per time bucket).
- Always apply value suppression post-noise for very small cohorts to avoid creating unique signals.

3) Data use & model-training risk
- Prohibit using raw or directly-identifying snapshot rows for ML training. ML may use only pseudonymized IDs and aggregated/DP-noised features. Require explicit product/legal signoff and data-processor contract if non-aggregated or sensitive features are used.
- For model training: require another RA review, and store training datasets in a separate controlled area with privacy review and provenance.

4) Storage & key management
- Encryption-at-rest: require DB encryption with CMEK/KMS where supported (CMEK for managed DBs). If DB cannot use CMEK, store snapshots in an encrypted column or a separate encrypted store with KMS-managed keys.
- Key rotation: rotate keys at least annually; for HMAC keys consider rotation every 90 days if operationally feasible. Implement key versioning so previous hashes can still be validated or rehashed in controlled migration.
- Storage segregation: store revenue_snapshots in a dedicated schema/DB with stricter ACLs, separate service accounts, and network segmentation.

5) Access controls & audit
- RBAC: restrict snapshot read access to explicit roles (reporting, finance, analytics) defined in a role catalog. No default developer access.
- Implement least-privilege views: create sanitized views that expose only aggregated/pseudonymized fields; deny direct table access.
- Auditing: audit all reads and exports (who, when, query id, purpose). Logs must NOT contain raw PII. If logging pseudonyms is necessary for debugging, log only truncated pseudonym hashes and treat logs as sensitive.

6) Migration/backfill risk
- Backfill pattern: perform backfills in small batches (e.g., <= 10k rows per batch or as system performance dictates), via a controlled job that writes directly to the target pseudonymized table. Do not write raw PII to intermediate persistent tables. Use ephemeral temp tables in memory or encrypted temp tables with strict ACLs and auto-destroy immediately after job completion.
- Rollback: have a reversible job that can delete newly-written rows by batch id and a dry-run mode for validation. Retain audit logs of the backfill job parameters.

7) Endpoint behavior & async/reporting
- Heavy/long queries: require async-only endpoints for heavy reporting; use the snapshots as canonical cache for heavy queries. Expose only sanitized/aggregated snapshots to users.
- Cache privacy: apply same access controls and TTLs to caches. Require access gating and record accesses.

8) Logging & telemetry
- Redact PII in logs; never log raw customer identifiers. For pseudonymized IDs, log truncated hashes (first N characters) only if necessary and mark logs as sensitive.
- Ensure all telemetry dimensions used for alerting are aggregated to non-identifying buckets. Add automated checks to CI that common logging paths don't serialize PII fields.

9) Retention policy
- Raw-identifying data: avoid persisting; if present for business reasons, limit to maximum 90 days and require legal/product justification.
- Pseudonymized snapshots: default retention 24 months for reporting/finance. Allow shorter retention (e.g., 12 months) for smaller tenants or higher-sensitivity contexts. Enforce automatic purge jobs (daily TTL sweeps) with immutability window documented.

B) Minimal Responsible-AI CI acceptance tests (to gate PR)
1) PII fields absent: unit/integration test asserting canonical test fixtures produce snapshot rows with no raw PII columns present (customer email/account_number/null).
2) Deterministic HMAC check: test that HMAC pseudonymization is deterministic (same input -> same output) and non-reversible (no key leak in test). Verify stored pseudonym length == expected and format.
3) Suppression rule: automated test that groups with count < k (k=10) are suppressed from output/export endpoints or flagged as masked.
4) Aggregation granularity: test that exported snapshots use minimum time bucket size per config (e.g., weekly for external) and reject finer buckets without override flag/approval.
5) Retention purge: integration test that TTL/purge job deletes rows older than retention policy and logs the purge event.
6) Backfill safety: backfill job test verifying no intermediate tables retain raw PII and that backfill runs in batches and records job audit metadata.
7) Logging check: static/assertion test that common loggers do not include PII field names; run sample queries and assert logs contain no identifiable strings.
8) KMS usage: test that pseudonymization path uses KMS key id (mockable) and fails if KMS not available (no fallback to insecure key).

C) Signoff and open concerns
- Conditional signoff: I provisionally approve proceeding with pseudonymization + suppression + retention controls as above, provided the implementation meets these requirements and Security/Arch enforce KMS key controls and RBAC. This approval is contingent on:
  a) Security validating KMS/CMEK integration and key access policy (no key material in app configs), and
  b) Product/legal confirming retention durations and permitted uses (esp. ML training) or explicitly documenting consent/legal basis.
- Open concerns requiring action before full merge:
  1) Decision needed on exact cohort threshold for public exports (10 vs 20) and epsilon if DP is adopted—product/legal to decide.
  2) Operational plan for key rotation and re-hashing strategy; Arch/Security must document key-version migration approach.
  3) Confirmation that logs and telemetry paths are sanitized by default and that analytics jobs will only use aggregated/pseudonymized inputs.

Priority items for Merger/Security/Arch to enforce before deploy: (i) KMS/CMEK enabled, (ii) schema separation + RBAC views enforced, (iii) suppression logic implemented and tested, (iv) retention purge job scheduled and validated.

Overall risk summary: Moderate — main residual risk is re-identification from small cohorts or correlated external data. Mitigations above (k>=10–20, DP for exports, pseudonymization, strict RBAC, retention limits) reduce risk to acceptable levels pending legal/product confirmation on retention and DP parameters.

Responsible-AI decision: send onward for Merger review and require Security+Arch to confirm KMS & RBAC controls; request product/legal to confirm retention & ML use policy prior to final merge.

Security review update for PR v2 'Implement standard-revenue calculation with privacy/KMS/RA updates':

Summary/Overall assessment:
- The v2 changes materially improve data protection posture (deterministic pseudonymization with KMS, schema separation, RBAC grants, k-anonymity enforcement, logging redaction, and additional docs/evidence). These address many earlier high-risk items. I can provisionally accept the design, but several architecture-level confirmations and a few fixes are required before Security can sign off for production deployment.

High-priority items requiring Arch validation / action before Merger deploy:
1) KMS/CMEK correctness & key lifecycle (must confirm):
   - Confirm no key material or long-lived plaintext keys are ever stored in app configs, logs, or CI. Use only KMS API calls for HMAC operations or key derivation as implemented; verify workload-identity/service-account auth used.
   - Confirm CMEK is enforced for the DB/storage used by revenue_snapshots and for any backup storage. Provide proof that CMEK is enabled and that key rotation is tested (docs/kms_rotation_plan.md is a good start).
   - Ensure kms_key_version_id is recorded for every pseudonymization operation and is immutable in audit logs for forensic key-version mapping.

2) Deterministic pseudonymizer cryptography (advise and validate):
   - HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 128 bits: collision probability acceptable for most reporting (2^-128); however, deterministic pseudonyms enable cross-dataset linking — confirm this is an acceptable privacy tradeoff with Data Protection/Privacy teams.
   - Recommend including a context/namespace string (e.g., service name + purpose) in the HMAC input to avoid cross-purpose collisions/reuse.
   - Ensure truncation is applied consistently and tests assert no collisions on realistic data volumes; provide analytic estimate of expected collision rate given max dataset size.

3) IAM & DB ACLs (must validate least-privilege):
   - Review and approve the IAM policies and service account permissions referenced in docs/evidence/rbac_policies.md; ensure the app can only call KMS with HMAC/crypto permissions, and cannot decrypt raw secrets.
   - Confirm DB grants in migration create a separate schema with strict GRANTs (revenue_admin vs revenue_analyst_readonly) and that production DB users/roles follow least-privilege. Consider enforcing row-level policies if further restriction needed.

4) Aggregation & suppression correctness (must validate server-side enforcement):
   - Confirm k-anonymity enforcement (default k=10) applies to the fully aggregated result prior to any pagination slicing or export. Ensure suppression is applied after combining all pages and across any groupings/time buckets.
   - Confirm minimum export granularity (weekly) and that the API rejects requests that would circumvent suppression by requesting tiny ranges or very small buckets.
   - Ensure tests explicitly cover page-level attacks (request many pages with small buckets to reconstruct suppressed groups) and that the server enforces global query limits to prevent reconstruction.

5) Input validation, query-cost limits & rate limiting (must implement if not present):
   - Enforce a server-side maximum date window (e.g., 3 months) and a hard max page_size (e.g., <=100). Default page_size should be small (e.g., 25).
   - Implement per-user and per-IP rate limits and/or quota for heavy reporting endpoints. Consider requiring elevated permissions for large/long-running queries and/or moving heavy work to async jobs that generate cached snapshots.
   - Add query-cost estimator or MAX_ROWS_SCAN guard to reject very expensive queries. Provide metrics to monitor query cost.

6) DB/ORM safety & migration/backfill safety (must validate migration plan):
   - Ensure all DB operations use parameterized ORM APIs or prepared statements; no raw SQL string concatenation in revenue_calculator or migration scripts.
   - Migration/backfill: must create table and indexes non-blocking, run backfill in small transactions with bounded batch sizes, and add indexes after data load where possible. Provide rollback steps and runbook (docs/backfill_rollback_plan.md exists; ensure it includes production run-playbook).

7) Snapshot storage, encryption-at-rest & access controls (must confirm):
   - Ensure revenue_snapshots never contain raw PII; only pseudonym + kms_key_version_id + aggregated metrics are allowed. If any identifiers are stored, they must be hashed/pseudonymized and access to the snapshot schema must be restricted.
   - Confirm DB-level encryption/keys (CMEK) and network-level protections (private DB subnet, no public access). Confirm backups/encrypted snapshots also use CMEK.

8) Logging & telemetry (verify config):
   - Confirm logs redact PII and payment fields and do not include request bodies that contain identifiers. Audit logs should contain only pseudonym + key version and event metadata.
   - Verify retention and access controls for audit logs; ensure they are immutable and monitored.

9) CI & test strategy for KMS (advise/validate):
   - CI must never use production KMS keys. Use mocked KMS in unit tests and either ephemeral test keys scoped to ephemeral projects or a KMS emulator for integration tests. Confirm gating so production KMS usage requires manual approval and environment-specific secrets are not exposed in CI logs.

10) Legal/retention signoff (blocking for prod):
   - Legal/Data-retention signoff (retention_signoff.pdf placeholder) is outstanding. Production deployment must not proceed until legal approves retention policy for pseudonymized snapshots and exports.

Acceptance criteria (concrete checklist Security requires before final Security-Stop -> StopSecurity to Merger):
- AuthZ: route enforces authentication + RBAC; unit/integration tests for 401/403 included.
- Pseudonymization: HMAC includes context/namespace; tests for collision probability and deterministic behavior added; kms_key_version_id recorded per row.
- KMS/CMEK: proof of CMEK enabled for DB/storage and documented KMS rotation + access controls; CI uses mocks/no-prod-keys.
- Aggregation/suppression: server-side suppression enforced globally (not per-page); tests for pagination attack vectors added.
- Input limits & rate limiting: server-side date window, page_size hard limit, rate-limiting/quota for heavy queries implemented and tested.
- Migration/backfill: documented non-blocking migration plan with batched backfill, rollback, and production runbook validated under load test.
- Logging: redaction verified; no PII in logs; audit logs contain only pseudonym and key version.
- Legal signoff: retention policy signed off by Legal/Privacy.
- Dependency SCA: run dependency-vuln scan and address any findings.

Recommended next steps for Architecture team:
- Validate KMS/CMEK architecture, key rotation, and key access boundaries. Confirm KEK/DEK model and ensure app uses only HMAC / sign operations and not decryption of raw material.
- Review DB network placement (private subnet), backup encryption, and whether revenue_snapshots should live in a separate DB instance/schema with tighter ACLs.
- Recommend adding an async batch pipeline for large queries and using precomputed snapshots for heavy reporting to minimize load on primary DB.
- Approve IAM policies and ensure service accounts have minimal KMS and DB privileges.

If Arch confirms the above items (especially KMS/CMEK proof, suppression enforcement, migration/backfill plan, and legal signoff), Security will mark this as approved to proceed. If any item cannot be satisfied, please return to Author/Quality with specifics and include mitigations and timeline.

I have forwarded these findings for architecture validation and await Arch's confirmation; once Arch confirms items above I will respond to Merger signals (AgainSecurity or StopSecurity).

payload:
Security update for PR v2 'Implement standard-revenue calculation' forwarded to Architecture. Security provisionally accepts v2 improvements but requires Architecture validation on several items; requesting Responsible-AI review focused on privacy/PII/re-identification risk and concrete acceptance criteria.

Please review and advise on the following items (deliverables requested: explicit recommendations, thresholds, retention durations, CI test checklist, and signoff or open concerns):

1) Deterministic pseudonymization
- Current approach: HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 128 bits per row, with kms_key_version_id recorded.
- Questions: Is deterministic HMAC (with context/namespace) acceptable vs stronger anonymization for our reporting use cases? Recommend whether to require a namespace/context string in HMAC input and whether truncation to 128 bits is acceptable. Provide guidance on acceptable truncation/collision tradeoffs and an analytic collision-rate estimate for expected dataset sizes.

2) Cross-dataset linking & re-identification risk
- Deterministic pseudonyms permit linking across datasets; advise whether this is permissible under our data protection posture. Recommend minimum cohort sizes (k), suppression/smoothing rules, and max granularity (time bucket size) to mitigate re-identification risk. Security suggests k=10 and weekly buckets; please confirm or propose alternatives.

3) Suppression & pagination attack protections
- Confirm suppression must be applied globally after aggregation (not per-page) and recommend strategies to prevent reconstruction via repeated/paginated queries (global query-cost limits, per-user quotas, enforced aggregation windows, response-level suppression/rounding, or differential privacy). Provide specific rules/tests to detect page-attack vectors.

4) Retention & purge policy
- Recommend retention durations for pseudonymized snapshots (e.g., 90 days, 1 year) and whether pseudonymized rows may be retained longer than raw PII. Specify automatic purge rules and proof/CI tests to validate purge runs.

5) Use for ML / analytics
- Advise whether snapshot data (pseudonymized) may be used for model training/analytics. If allowed, specify additional anonymization or data minimization requirements or explicit consent/legal basis needed.

6) KMS context, key-version, and auditability
- Confirm storing kms_key_version_id per row is privacy-preserving and helpful for forensics. Recommend whether key-version must be immutable and included in audit logs, and any constraints on exposing key-version in logs/exports.

7) CI/test guidance for KMS & pseudonymization
- Recommend CI practices: mocked KMS/emulator or ephemeral test keys (never use prod keys in CI). Provide minimal CI/QA acceptance tests for pseudonymizer correctness and non-reversibility assumptions.

8) Acceptance-test checklist for RA gating (suggested items to add to CI)
- Snapshot rows from canonical fixtures contain no raw PII fields.
- Pseudonymization deterministic + non-reversible checks and collision probability test on realistic fixture scale.
- Global suppression enforced for small cohorts; tests for pagination-reconstruction attack.
- Retention purge job runs and deletes expired pseudonymized rows in test env.
- Audit logs record access events with pseudonym and kms_key_version_id only (no raw PII).

9) Any open privacy/legal blockers
- Note Security flagged outstanding Legal/retention signoff before prod. Confirm whether RA/legal signoff is required now and what conditions are needed for signoff.

Requested response
- For each numbered item above, please provide: (A) concrete recommendation (algorithms/params/thresholds), (B) rationale/risks, (C) a short CI test checklist we can add, and (D) an explicit signoff or list of unresolved concerns blocking prod.

Rationale: Architecture needs Responsible-AI confirmation on privacy tradeoffs (deterministic pseudonymization, k-anonymity thresholds, retention, ML usage, and CI tests) to satisfy Security's acceptance criteria and allow Merger/DevOps to proceed.

label: ToMerger
payload:
Responsible-AI review (detailed answers per Arch items 1–9) for PR 'Implement standard-revenue calculation'. For each item I provide: (A) concrete recommendation (algorithms/params/thresholds), (B) rationale/risks, (C) CI/test checklist items, and (D) signoff or unresolved concerns.

1) Deterministic pseudonymization
A) Recommendation
- Continue using HMAC-SHA256 with explicit context/namespace prepended to input (e.g., data = tenant_id || '::' || purpose || '::' || customer_id). Namespace must include purpose (reporting, analytics, export) so tokens for different uses are not linkable by accident.
- Truncate to 128 bits (16 bytes) is acceptable for operational datasets; store as base64 or hex. Record kms_key_version_id in metadata for each row.
- Use KMS-managed symmetric key (CMEK) for HMAC; enforce deterministic mode only for pseudonymization/joins; never use deterministic keys for anything else.

B) Rationale / risks
- Deterministic HMAC enables necessary joinability across systems but permits cross-dataset linking. 128-bit output space gives extremely low collision probability for realistic N. Collision probability ~ N^2/(2 * 2^128). For N=1e9 rows, collision probability ~1e-21 (negligible). Risk remains primarily re-identification via linkage, not collisions.

C) CI/test checklist
- Deterministic test: same input -> same pseudonym; different context -> different pseudonym.
- Collision simulation: run property test over synthetic fixture (e.g., 10M distinct inputs) and assert no collisions (or assert collision rate below threshold). Use smaller test sizes but scale analytically in CI notes.
- Ensure kms_key_version_id recorded for each generated pseudonym in test metadata.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- Signoff on deterministic HMAC + 128-bit truncation conditioned on namespace inclusion and KMS controls. Unresolved: product decision whether single global namespace is allowed vs per-purpose namespaces (I recommend per-purpose namespaces; Arch/Product to confirm).

2) Cross-dataset linking & re-identification risk
A) Recommendation
- Allow deterministic linking only when needed and under strict RBAC/audit. Require per-purpose namespace to limit accidental linking.
- Cohort thresholds: internal uses: k >= 10; external/public exports: k >= 20. For tenants with small populations, use coarser time buckets (weekly/monthly) or disallow fine-grained exports.
- Time granularity: internal dashboards may use daily only if cohort sizes remain >= k; external exports should default to weekly (7d) or monthly for small tenants.

B) Rationale / risks
- Deterministic tokens let adversaries cross-reference with other datasets (external breach or public data). k-anonymity reduces risk but does not eliminate it for unique attribute combinations—thus combine suppression with coarser granularity and/or differential privacy for exports.

C) CI/test checklist
- Tests that any exported query with group_count < k is suppressed/blocked.
- Tests enforcing minimum bucket size for export endpoints per tenant profile.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- Conditional signoff with k=10 internal, k=20 external; product/legal must confirm threshold for public exports and whether some tenants require stricter bounds.

3) Suppression & pagination attack protections
A) Recommendation
- Always apply suppression globally after full-aggregation step, before pagination; suppression decisions must be computed on the full result set, not per page.
- Prevent reconstruction via pagination by enforcing aggregation-first API design: server computes and applies suppression/rounding/noise, stores the sanitized result set, and pages the sanitized result to the client.
- Additional protections: per-client query quotas, global query-cost budget, disallow multi-attribute filtering that yields groups smaller than k, and require server-side query planners to reject queries that would produce small cohorts.
- For higher-sensitivity exports, apply response rounding (e.g., round counts to nearest multiple of 5) or DP (Laplace or discrete Gaussian) with epsilon <= 1 for external exports.

B) Rationale / risks
- Pagination-reconstruction is a common vector: attackers page through fine-grained slices to isolate single individuals. Global suppression and server-side sanitization eliminate that vector. Rounding/DP reduces risk further.

C) CI/test checklist
- Test that suppression is applied when result set aggregated server-side and that paginated responses do not bypass suppression.
- Attack simulation test: issue paginated queries slicing along allowed dimensions and assert no incremental disclosure (no singletons appear across pages).
- Rate/quota enforcement tests.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- Approve suppression global-after-aggregation with server-side sanitized paging. Unresolved: whether DP will be used for all external exports; product/legal to sign off DP parameters.

4) Retention & purge policy
A) Recommendation
- Raw PII: do not persist. If unavoidable, limit to ≤ 90 days and only with explicit legal/product justification.
- Pseudonymized snapshots: default retention 24 months (2 years) for reporting/finance. Allow configuration per-tenant/sensitivity down to 12 months. For high-risk tenants or datasets, default to 12 months.
- Implement automatic purge job that runs daily and deletes rows older than retention window; mark purged batches in audit log with job id, row counts, and kms_key_version_id used.

B) Rationale / risks
- Longer retention increases re-identification risk over time and amplifies linkage possibilities. Two-year retention balances business needs and privacy risk; shorter is better where feasible.

C) CI/test checklist
- Integration test that purge job removes rows older than retention config and writes audit event.
- Test that retention config per-tenant applies correctly.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- Conditional signoff for 24 months default; product/legal must confirm acceptable retention windows and any contractual requirements for specific tenants.

5) Use for ML / analytics
A) Recommendation
- Prohibit using raw or reversible pseudonymized rows for ML training without an explicit RA/product/legal review. Permitted training data must be: (a) aggregated summaries, (b) DP-noised features with documented epsilon, or (c) per-purpose pseudonyms that prevent cross-dataset re-linking and are approved by legal.
- For any ML use of pseudonymized IDs, require data minimization, lineage tracking, and storage in a separate, access-restricted training dataset store.

B) Rationale / risks
- ML models can memorize and leak PII; training on per-subject time-series increases re-identification risk. DP or strong aggregation reduces risk.

C) CI/test checklist
- Policy enforcement test: attempts to export raw snapshot rows to model-training path should fail in CI unless an approval artifact is present.
- Check that training dataset creation pipeline only accepts allowed inputs (aggregated/DP) and logs approvals.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- No signoff to allow arbitrary ML use. ML usage allowed only after explicit legal/product approval and an RA review of the proposed training dataset.

6) KMS context, key-version, and auditability
A) Recommendation
- Storing kms_key_version_id per row is acceptable and recommended for forensics. Key version should be immutable for existing rows (i.e., do not change existing row metadata); new rows get the new key version.
- Include kms_key_version_id in internal audit logs (not user-facing exports). Do not include raw key material anywhere.
- Key rotation: plan and document rotation strategy. For HMAC pseudonyms, support key-versioned verification or controlled re-hashing migration when a key is retired.

B) Rationale / risks
- Key-version metadata aids incident response and migration. Exposing key-version is low risk compared to key material but still should be limited to internal logs and admin views.

C) CI/test checklist
- Test that every pseudonymized row includes kms_key_version_id in metadata.
- Test key rotation behavior in staging: new rows use new version; old rows retain old version metadata and verify lookups still work.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- Signoff on storing kms_key_version_id internally. Unresolved: detailed rotation timetable and migration procedure — Arch/Security to provide documented process.

7) CI/test guidance for KMS & pseudonymization
A) Recommendation
- CI must never use production keys. Use a KMS emulator or ephemeral test keys with restricted privileges. Mock KMS calls in unit tests and provide integration tests against an emulator.
- Ensure CI asserts failure when KMS is unavailable (no insecure fallback permitted).

B) Rationale / risks
- Using real keys in CI is a severe secret-exposure risk. Emulator allows behavior testing without key leakage.

C) CI/test checklist
- Mocked KMS unit tests verifying correct HMAC invocation and deterministic output.
- Integration test against KMS emulator verifying key_version presence and that pipeline fails when emulator not present.
- Test that pseudonymizer rejects plaintext key injection or fallback to insecure local keys.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- Signoff on these CI constraints. Unresolved: select and provision a KMS emulator solution for CI (Security/DevOps to finalize).

8) Acceptance-test checklist for RA gating (concrete items for CI)
A) Recommendation (list to add to CI)
- Snapshot rows from canonical fixtures contain no raw PII fields (email, account_number, phone, address, customer_id) in persisted snapshots.
- Pseudonymization deterministic: same input -> same output; context-sensitivity: different purpose -> different token.
- Collision probability sanity check for synthetic loads (e.g., assert zero collisions for 1M distinct inputs in test run; document analytic estimate for production scale).
- Global suppression enforced: any group with count < k is suppressed; tests for pagination-resistance (simulate attacker paging across slices).
- Retention purge job removes expired rows and logs purge metadata.
- Audit logs record access events (who/when/query id/kms_key_version_id) and logs are validated to contain no raw PII.
- KMS usage tests: pseudonymizer uses KMS key version; CI fails if KMS not available or if fallback key used.

B) Rationale / risks
- These tests ensure the implementation enforces the main privacy controls and prevent regressions.

C) Signoff / unresolved
- Signoff conditional on all above tests being implemented in CI. Unresolved: specific collision-test scale and exact k values for public export (product/legal decision).

9) Open privacy/legal blockers
A) Recommendation & list
- Legal/product must explicitly confirm: (a) retention windows (default 24 months or alternative), (b) acceptable cohort thresholds for public exports (k=10 vs k=20), and (c) whether deterministic linking across datasets is permitted for business cases.
- Decide whether DP will be required for public exports and choose epsilon (recommended <=1 for external; <=0.5 for highly-sensitive).

B) Rationale / risks
- These are policy decisions that materially affect acceptable risk; RA cannot unilaterally set legal/contractual parameters.

C) CI/test checklist
- Gate CI to fail merges if the PR does not include a documented retention config and a documented product/legal approval artifact for any non-default choices.

D) Signoff / unresolved
- No final signoff until product/legal confirms retention and export policy and until Security confirms KMS/CMEK and key rotation operational plan.

Overall Responsible-AI decision (summary)
- Conditional approval to proceed with implementing HMAC-SHA256 pseudonymization truncated to 128 bits, per-purpose namespace, kms_key_version_id recorded, global suppression (k>=10 internal, k>=20 external), server-side aggregation-before-pagination, retention purge (default 24 months), and strict ML usage controls — PROVIDED that Security/Arch implement KMS/CMEK, RBAC/schema separation, and Product/Legal confirm retention and export thresholds (k/DP epsilon). CI must include the tests listed above.

Priority items for Merger/Security/Arch before merge/deploy
1) Confirm Product/Legal decisions: retention windows and public export thresholds (k and DP epsilon).
2) Confirm KMS/CMEK availability and key policy (no prod keys in CI, rotation plan documented).
3) Implement server-side global suppression and pagination-safe APIs; add suppression/rate-limiting tests.
4) Add the RA CI gating tests listed above; ensure no flaky path that allows raw PII to persist.

Residual risk: Moderate (primary vector is linkage/re-identification from deterministic tokens and small cohorts). The combination of per-purpose namespaces, RBAC, global suppression, DP for exports, and retention limits reduces this to acceptable operational risk if the outstanding product/legal/KMS items are closed.

If Merger wants, I can convert these items into a concise checklist PR comment and the exact CI test specs (test names, expected assertions, and mock patterns) for developers to implement.

- Logging check: static/assert tests ensuring loggers don’t include PII fields; run sample queries and assert logs exclude identifiers.

If any product/legal decisions (retention windows, public-cohort threshold k, DP epsilon) deviate from defaults above, attach explicit product/legal signoff.

11) Re-request reviewers

label: ToMerger
payload:
Responsible-AI formal responses to Arch items 1–9 for PR 'Implement standard-revenue calculation'. For each item I give: (A) recommendation (algorithm/params/thresholds), (B) rationale/risks, (C) minimal CI tests (short), and (D) explicit signoff (Yes/No and conditions).

1) Deterministic pseudonymization & truncation
A) Recommendation
- Continue HMAC-SHA256(context: tenant_id::purpose::customer_id) but require an explicit per-purpose namespace/prefix in the HMAC input (purpose ∈ {reporting, analytics, export, training}) to reduce accidental linking. Use the KMS-managed symmetric HMAC key. Truncate output to 128 bits (16 bytes) and encode hex/base64. Persist kms_key_version_id per row.
- If any export/use requires cryptographic-strength non-linkability, use full 256-bit output or switch to per-use keyed encryption or DP aggregates for that pipeline.
B) Rationale / risks
- Deterministic HMAC is required for joinability. 128-bit truncation yields negligible collision risk for expected cardinalities (collision approx N^2/(2*2^128)). Example: for N=1e9 rows, collision probability ≈ 1e-21 — effectively zero. Main risk is re-identification via cross-dataset linking, not collisions.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Determinism: same input+namespace -> same pseudonym; different namespace -> different pseudonym.
- Collision sanity: run synthetic test (e.g., 1M distinct inputs) asserting zero collisions; CI documents analytic extrapolation to production scale.
- kms_key_version present: every pseudonymized row has kms_key_version_id metadata.
D) Signoff
- Yes, conditional: signoff granted for HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 128 bits provided per-purpose namespace is enforced and KMS access controls/rotation are implemented and documented.

2) Cross-dataset linking & re-identification risk
A) Recommendation
- Approve Security's defaults but make them policy: internal exports k >= 10; external/public exports k >= 20. Default min time bucket: internal — daily (only if cohort >= k), external — weekly. For small tenants, auto-fallback to monthly or disable fine-grained exports.
- For any public or high-risk export, require DP or stronger aggregation (recommended Laplace with epsilon <= 1 for external; epsilon <= 0.5 for highly sensitive).
B) Rationale / risks
- These thresholds balance utility and privacy. Deterministic pseudonyms enable linking so suppression + coarser buckets + DP are needed to reduce re-id risk. k-anonymity alone is imperfect but useful when combined with other controls.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Export endpoint test: any export that would produce a group_count < k must be suppressed/blocked.
- Bucket enforcement: tests that reject requests for buckets smaller than allowed for tenant profile.
D) Signoff
- Conditional Yes: approve k=10 internal / k=20 external as baseline, subject to product/legal confirmation for public exports (they may choose stricter options per contract/tenant).

3) Global suppression & pagination-attack mitigations
A) Recommendation
- Enforce global suppression computed on full-aggregation results, before pagination. Implement server-side sanitization/aggregation-first APIs that compute sanitized results and then paginate. Add per-user query quotas and global query-cost budgets. For higher sensitivity, add rounding or DP on top of suppression.
B) Rationale / risks
- Pagination or incremental querying is a high-risk reconstruction vector. Server-side aggregation + suppression prevents per-page leakage. Quotas and query-cost limits reduce exploratory attacks.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Pagination-resistance test: simulate attacker issuing paginated queries across slices; assert no singleton disclosures across pages and no incremental information gain beyond sanitized result.
- Quota/enforcement tests: assert per-user and global quota enforcement when thresholds exceeded.
D) Signoff
- Yes, provided aggregation-first, suppression-before-pagination, and quota enforcement are implemented and tested. Recommend adding DP/rounding for public exports (product/legal to confirm DP parameters).

4) Retention & purge policy
A) Recommendation
- Raw PII: do not persist. If retained for business/legal reasons, max retention <= 90 days and require documented legal/product justification.
- Pseudonymized snapshots: default retention = 24 months. Allow tenant-specific overrides to as low as 12 months for higher-risk customers. Implement daily automatic purge job that deletes rows older than retention window; record purge job id, row counts, and kms_key_version_id in an audit event.
B) Rationale / risks
- Longer retention increases linkage and re-identification risk. 24 months is a practical compromise for reporting while keeping risk moderate; shorter retention is safer where possible.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Purge job test: create rows with varied timestamps; run purge job; assert rows older than TTL removed and purge log entry exists with counts and key_version.
- Tenant retention config test: per-tenant TTL honored.
D) Signoff
- Conditional Yes: can proceed with default 24 months but final signoff requires Product/Legal confirmation of retention policy for production; RA requires documented exception approvals for any longer retention.

5) Use for ML/analytics
A) Recommendation
- Prohibit direct use of raw pseudonymized rows for ML training without RA + Legal + Product approval. Allowed ML inputs: aggregated summaries, DP-noised features with documented epsilon, or per-purpose pseudonyms that are cryptographically isolated (different namespace/keys) and approved. Store training data in a separate, access-controlled repository with lineage and approval artifacts.
B) Rationale / risks
- ML models can memorize and leak PII; longitudinal time-series exacerbate risk. Controls and approvals reduce legal/regulatory and privacy risks.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Export-to-training guard: CI test that attempts to export raw snapshot rows to model-training path fails unless an approval artifact (signed config) is present.
- Training-data provenance test: pipeline rejects datasets lacking lineage and approval metadata.
D) Signoff
- No: cannot approve ML use of snapshot rows generally. Approve only on a case-by-case basis after RA/legal/product review and with required mitigations in place.

6) KMS metadata & auditability
A) Recommendation
- Approve storing kms_key_version_id per row and including it in internal audit logs; do not expose key-version to external exports. Make key_version immutable for historical rows. Maintain key-access audit trails and restrict access to key-version metadata to privileged admin/audit roles.
B) Rationale / risks
- kms_key_version_id aids incident response and supports key rotation strategies. Exposing only the version (not key material) presents low privacy risk but should be access-restricted.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Metadata presence test: every pseudonymized row includes kms_key_version_id.
- Key rotation test: simulate rotation in staging; verify new rows use new version and old rows retain old version for lookups.
D) Signoff
- Yes, approve storing kms_key_version_id internally and in audit logs; require Security to document rotation/migration procedure before prod.

7) CI/test guidance for pseudonymizer & KMS
A) Recommendation
- Do NOT use production keys in CI. Use a KMS emulator or ephemeral test keys. Unit tests should mock KMS; integration tests can use emulator. CI must assert failure if KMS not available; no insecure local fallback allowed.
B) Rationale / risks
- Production key leakage is a severe risk. Emulators/mock ensure behavior tests without secret exposure.
C) CI tests (minimal)
- Mocked unit tests for deterministic HMAC behavior and error paths when KMS fails.
- Integration test against emulator validating kms_key_version_id and failure on emulator unavailability.
D) Signoff
- Yes, provided emulator/mocking is used and CI prohibits real keys. DevOps/Security to provide emulator choice and CI secret management guidance.

8) Acceptance-test checklist for RA gating (machine-friendly brief list)
- RA-1: NoRawPII: canonical fixtures -> persisted snapshots contain no raw PII columns (email, phone, account_number, address, raw customer_id).
- RA-2: DeterministicHMAC: same input+namespace -> same token; different namespace -> different token. kms_key_version_id present.
- RA-3: CollisionSanity: synthetic test N=1e6 assert zero collisions; analytic collision estimate documented for production scale.
- RA-4: SuppressionEnforced: any output/export where group_count < k is suppressed. (k config: internal=10, external=20)
- RA-5: PaginationResistance: server-side aggregation -> sanitized result pages; simulated paginated attack returns no incremental disclosures.
- RA-6: RetentionPurge: purge job deletes rows older than TTL; purge audit event present with counts and key_version.
- RA-7: KMSUsage: pseudonymizer uses KMS key version; CI fails if KMS missing or fallback used.
- RA-8: MLGuard: attempts to export raw rows to training path fail unless signed approval artifact present.
Pass/Fail criteria: tests must return PASS for all RA-* tests for CI gate to allow merge.

9) Legal/Privacy signoff
A) Requirements for Legal/Privacy before full prod signoff
- Product/Legal must explicitly approve: (a) retention default (we recommend 24 months or tenant-specific shorter), (b) public export cohort threshold (accept k=20 or higher), (c) whether DP is mandatory for external/public exports and specify epsilon, and (d) allowed ML usage cases and consent/legal basis.
B) RA stance
- RA cannot provide final legal signoff. RA provides technical conditional approval given above controls, but final go/no-go requires Legal/Privacy confirmation of retention and export policies.
C) CI gating
- CI must gate merges if PR lacks documented Product/Legal approval artifact for non-default retention or export thresholds.
D) Signoff
- No final legal signoff from RA; require Legal/Privacy signoff itemized above before production.

Open concerns that block prod (short list with mitigation/timeline)
1) Product/Legal retention & export policy (blocking): need explicit decisions on retention windows and public/export thresholds (k and DP epsilon). Mitigation: fast-track Product/Legal review; timeline 3 business days if prioritized.
2) Key rotation & KMS ops plan (blocking): Security must publish rotation/migration procedures (how to verify/rehash old rows). Mitigation: Security to deliver rotation doc and staging runbook; timeline 5 business days.
3) CI KMS emulator provisioning (blocking for safe testing): DevOps/Security to provision emulator and update CI to reject prod-keys; timeline 3–7 days depending on environment.
4) Suppression + pagination implementation + tests (blocking): dev team to implement aggregation-first API and add pagination-resistance tests from RA-5; timeline depend on effort – estimate 2–5 days of engineering work for initial implementation and tests.

Compact machine-readable acceptance checklist (JSON string you can paste into CI):
{"RA_checks":[{"id":"RA-1","name":"NoRawPII","assert":"snapshot rows contain no raw PII fields"},{"id":"RA-2","name":"DeterministicHMAC","assert":"same input+namespace => same token; kms_key_version present"},{"id":"RA-3","name":"CollisionSanity","assert":"synthetic 1e6 inputs -> zero collisions; analytic extrapolation attached"},{"id":"RA-4","name":"SuppressionEnforced","assert":"exports with group_count < k are suppressed (configurable k)"},{"id":"RA-5","name":"PaginationResistance","assert":"paginated queries return only sanitized results; attack simulation passes"},{"id":"RA-6","name":"RetentionPurge","assert":"purge job removes expired rows and writes audit event"},{"id":"RA-7","name":"KMSUsage","assert":"pseudonymizer uses KMS key_version; CI fails if KMS missing; no prod keys in CI"},{"id":"RA-8","name":"MLGuard","assert":"raw snapshot export to training path blocked without signed approval"}]}

Final RA decision summary
- Conditional Approval: I approve progressing to implementation and Security/Arch validation with the controls above. Full production signoff is conditional on: (a) Product/Legal confirming retention and export thresholds, (b) Security publishing KMS rotation/migration plan and enabling CMEK/KMS, and (c) CI implementing the RA acceptance-test checklist and using KMS emulator (no prod keys in CI).

If helpful I can convert this into a short checklist comment for the PR and produce skeleton test code (test names, inputs, expected assertions) for developers to drop into the CI pipeline.

payload:
Responsible-AI formal response to Arch/Security v4 — per-item answers (1–9), CI tests, machine-readable acceptance checklist, and explicit signoff/next-blockers.

1) Cryptography & truncation
A) Recommendation
- Approve deterministic HMAC-SHA256 with explicit context tenant_id::purpose::customer_id and require per-purpose namespace (purpose ∈ {reporting, analytics, export, training}). Truncate to 128 bits (16 bytes) encoded hex/base64 and record kms_key_version_id per row. Use KMS-managed symmetric HMAC key (CMEK).
- If a pipeline requires stronger non-linkability, use full 256-bit HMAC output or per-use keyed encryption / DP aggregates for that pipeline.
B) Rationale/risks
- Deterministic HMAC is needed for joinability; 128-bit truncation gives negligible collision risk for expected scales. Main residual risk is re-identification via cross-dataset linking, not collision.
- Collision estimate: P(collision) ≈ N^2/(2*2^128). For N=1e9, P ≈ 1e-21; for N=1e7, P ≈ 1e-35 — effectively zero.
C) CI/test artifacts (exacts)
- Test: PSEUD-DET-001 (Determinism) — same input+namespace => same token; different namespace => different token. PASS if true for canonical fixture.
- Test: PSEUD-COLL-001 (Collision Sanity) — generate 1e6 synthetic distinct inputs in CI-stage run; assert zero collisions; attach analytic extrapolation for prod scale. PASS if zero collisions and analytic doc present.
- Test: PSEUD-META-001 — every pseudonymized row includes kms_key_version_id. PASS if metadata present for all rows.
D) Signoff
- YES (conditional). Conditions: per-purpose namespace enforced; KMS access controls, key-rotation plan & CMEK enabled and documented; no prod keys in CI.

2) Cross-dataset linking / re-identification risk
A) Recommendation
- Adopt Security’s thresholds as organizational baseline: internal uses: k >= 10; external/public exports: k >= 20. External exports default to weekly buckets; fall back to monthly for small tenants. Require DP (Laplace/discrete Gaussian) for public-facing exports if product/legal decide to mandate (recommended epsilon <=1 external; <=0.5 for high-sensitivity).
B) Rationale/risks
- k-anonymity reduces risk but is not foolproof; combining suppression, coarser time buckets and optional DP lowers re-identification risk from deterministic tokens.
C) CI/tests
- Test: SUPP-EXPORT-001 — Export-request simulation returns suppression if any group_count < k (k paramized by env). PASS if suppressed.
- Test: BUCKET-ENF-001 — Request for finer-than-allowed bucket returns 400/blocked. PASS if blocked.
D) Signoff
- YES (conditional). Condition: Product/Legal confirms thresholds for public exports or requests higher k/DP parameters.

3) Global suppression & pagination-attack mitigations
A) Recommendation
- Enforce global suppression after full aggregation, before pagination. Implement aggregation-first server API that computes sanitized resultsets and pages sanitized results. Add per-user and global query quotas and a global query-cost budget. For sensitive external exports, add rounding or DP on top of suppression.
B) Rationale/risks
- Prevents reconstruction via paginated incremental queries; quotas reduce probing attacks. Rounding/DP reduces residual risk of unique signals.
C) CI/tests (attack detection)
- Test: PAG-RESIST-001 (Pagination Reconstruction) — simulate attacker issuing many paginated, sliced queries; PASS if no page returns a singleton and aggregated sanitized result equals server-stored sanitized result.
- Test: QUOTA-001 — per-user quota enforcement triggers 429 after threshold; PASS if 429 returned and subsequent queries blocked for window.
D) Signoff
- YES (conditional). Must implement server-side aggregation-first behavior and the two tests above. Recommend DP/rounding for public exports (product/legal decision on epsilon).

4) Retention & purge policy
A) Recommendation
- Raw PII: do not persist; if unavoidable, ≤ 90 days with legal/product approval. Pseudonymized snapshots default retention = 24 months; allow tenant-specific override down to 12 months. Daily purge job to delete rows older than TTL; log purge event with job_id, row_count, kms_key_version_id summary.
B) Rationale/risks
- Longer retention increases cumulative re-identification risk. 24 months balances business needs and privacy; shorter preferred for high-risk tenants.
C) CI/tests (purge behavior)
- Test: PURGE-001 — create rows with timestamps older/newer than TTL; run purge; PASS if rows older than TTL removed and purge audit event present with counts and key_version summary.
- Test: PURGE-RT-001 (performance) — in test env remove X% (e.g., 100%) of rows older than TTL within Y minutes (Y depends on size; for CI small dataset Y <= 2 minutes). PASS if deletion and log occur.
D) Signoff
- YES (conditional). Product/Legal must confirm default retention or provide per-tenant requirements; RA requires documented exceptions for any retention >24 months.

5) Use for ML / analytics
A) Recommendation
- Prohibit use of raw or reversible pseudonymized rows for ML without RA + Legal + Product approval. Permitted: aggregated summaries, DP-noised features (document epsilon), or per-purpose isolated pseudonyms with approval. Training datasets must be stored in a separate access-controlled repository with documented lineage and approval artifact.
B) Rationale/risks
- ML models can memorize and leak PII; longitudinal snapshot data increases risk. Approval and governance reduce compliance/privacy risk.
C) CI/tests (policy enforcement)
- Test: ML-GATE-001 — attempt to export raw snapshot rows into training pipeline; PASS if rejected unless signed approval artifact present.
- Test: ML-LINEAGE-001 — training dataset ingestion requires lineage and approval metadata; PASS if ingestion blocked when metadata missing.
D) Signoff
- NO general signoff. ML usage allowed only case-by-case after RA + Legal + Product reviews and controls in place.

6) KMS metadata & auditability
A) Recommendation
- Approve storing kms_key_version_id per row and including in internal audit logs. Do NOT expose kms_key_version_id in user-facing exports. Keep key_version immutable in row metadata; new rows record new key_version. Restrict access to key_version metadata to privileged admin/audit roles.
B) Rationale/risks
- Key-version aids forensics and migration; exposing version metadata internally is low risk but must be access-limited.
C) CI/tests
- Test: KMS-META-001 — every pseudonymized row includes kms_key_version_id. PASS if present.
- Test: KMS-ROT-001 — simulate key rotation in staging; verify new rows use new key_version and old rows retain old version; PASS if verified and lookup functions still succeed.
D) Signoff
- YES (conditional). Security must provide documented rotation/migration procedure before prod.

7) CI/test guidance for KMS & pseudonymizer
A) Recommendation
- CI must never use production keys. Use KMS emulator or ephemeral test keys. Unit tests mock KMS; integration tests against emulator. CI must fail if KMS emulator unavailable; no insecure local fallbacks.
B) Rationale/risks
- Prevents secret leakage and ensures pseudonymizer behavior tested without prod keys.
C) CI/tests
- Test: KMS-MOCK-001 — unit mocks verify correct HMAC invocation, deterministic output, and error handling when KMS fails. PASS if mocks exercised and behavior correct.
- Test: KMS-EMUL-001 — integration against emulator asserts kms_key_version_id present and pipeline fails when emulator unavailable. PASS if emulator present and tests pass; CI must error if emulator not provisioned.
D) Signoff
- YES (conditional). DevOps/Security must provision emulator and CI update; CI must forbid prod-key steps.

8) Concrete RA acceptance-test checklist (machine-readable JSON)
{"RA_checks":[
 {"id":"RA-1","name":"NoRawPII","assert":"persisted snapshots contain no raw PII fields (email, phone, account_number, address, raw customer_id)","pass":"no raw PII columns present in canonical fixture output"},
 {"id":"RA-2","name":"DeterministicHMAC","assert":"same input+namespace => same token; different namespace => different token; kms_key_version present","pass":"tokens deterministic and namespaces differ"},
 {"id":"RA-3","name":"CollisionSanity","assert":"synthetic 1e6 inputs -> zero collisions; analytic extrapolation for prod scale","pass":"zero collisions in synthetic run and analytic doc attached"},
 {"id":"RA-4","name":"SuppressionEnforced","assert":"exports with group_count < k suppressed (configurable k)","pass":"requests producing groups < k are suppressed/blocked"},
 {"id":"RA-5","name":"PaginationResistance","assert":"paginated queries return only sanitized results; simulated paginated attack returns no incremental disclosures","pass":"no singleton or incremental disclosures observed in attack simulation"},
 {"id":"RA-6","name":"RetentionPurge","assert":"purge job removes expired rows and writes audit event","pass":"rows older than TTL removed; purge audit event exists"},
 {"id":"RA-7","name":"KMSUsage","assert":"pseudonymizer uses KMS key_version; CI fails if KMS missing; no prod keys in CI","pass":"kvs present and CI disallows prod keys"},
 {"id":"RA-8","name":"MLGuard","assert":"raw snapshot export to training path blocked without signed approval","pass":"raw export attempts blocked unless approval artifact present"}
]}

Pass/fail: all RA_checks must PASS for CI gate.

9) Privacy/Legal signoff
A) RA decision
- RA cannot itself provide final Legal/Privacy signoff. RA issues CONDITIONAL approval for prod readiness, contingent on the following outstanding items delivered/validated:
  1) Product/Legal explicit approval of retention policy (default 24 months or approved alternative) and of public-export cohort threshold (k and DP epsilon). ETA: 3 business days if prioritized.
  2) Security provides documented KMS/CMEK key-rotation and migration procedure (how to re-hash / verify old tokens) and demonstrates CMEK enabled in staging. ETA: 5 business days.
  3) DevOps/Security provision KMS emulator and update CI so no prod keys used; RA acceptance tests integrated. ETA: 3–7 business days depending on infra.
  4) Developers implement aggregation-first API with suppression-before-pagination and provide PAG-RESIST-001 test. ETA: 2–5 business days.
B) Final Signoff Yes/No
- RA gives CONDITIONAL YES to proceed toward final infra validation and Security proofing; FINAL production signoff = NO until Product/Legal and Security deliver items above and CI RA_checks all PASS.

Summary of blockers (short)
- Product/Legal retention & public-export DP/threshold decision (blocking). ETA ~3 days.
- Security key rotation/migration runbook & CMEK enabled (blocking). ETA ~5 days.
- CI KMS emulator provisioning and CI update (blocking). ETA 3–7 days.
- Implementation and tests for suppression/pagination-resistance (blocking until tests present). ETA 2–5 days.

If Merger/Arch/Security would like, I will produce ready-to-drop test skeletons (test names, inputs, assertions, mock patterns) for each RA_check to speed CI implementation.
